subject: Post-call: inference readiness map + procurement asks
messages:
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Liam Ortega <liam@emuhealth.ai>; Priya Singh <psingh@emuhealth.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call: inference readiness map + procurement asks

Thanks again for taking the call today — really appreciated the context on Emu's onboarding flow and the hard latency/cost constraints you outlined. Below is a concise record of what we heard, our proposed technical starting points, and the immediate next steps so your procurement and engineering teams can move quickly.

What we heard (pain points / goals):
- SLO: 95th pctl latency <= 120ms end-to-end for single-turn clinical triage prompts (~180 tokens average).
- Throughput: peak spiky traffic ~220 QPS during morning triage window, baseline ~35 QPS.
- Token profile: average request ~180 tokens, average response ~220 tokens.
- Cost sensitivity: target inference cost ~<= $0.002 per full request (tokens in + out); procurement needs a pilot-priced commitment.
- Security: customer data must remain in-region (US) and be encrypted at rest; potential requirement for Private deployment later.

Redwood proposed starting configuration (high level):
- Model family: a 13B instruction-tuned open model (we recommended Redwood-13B quantized to 4-bit for cost/latency balance).
- Serving mode: Dedicated pool for pilot (predictable throughput and isolation) with fallback to Hosted API for burst capacity.
- Hardware baseline: mixed A10G for econ nodes + 1 H100 headroom for warm failover; final sizing suggested below.
- Performance levers: KV-prefix caching for common prompts, continuous batching at 25-40ms batch windows, and request-level routing with regional affinity.

Immediate engineering asks (what we need from Emu):
1) A sample traffic trace (1 week of anonymized timestamps + token lengths) or representative CSV — to validate batching assumptions.
2) Confirmation whether prompts include user PHI that would require private/on-premise deployment or stricter retention policies.
3) Primary SLA contact for procurement and security (name + email).

Next steps / owners: 
- Jonas Weber (Redwood) — I'll hand off capacity sketch and latency math (see Jonas' message below) by EOD tomorrow.
- Kimberly Park (Redwood) — I'll coordinate pilot commercial terms and produce a pilot quote (attached spreadsheet) by Monday.
- Liam / Priya (Emu) — please send the traffic extract and security contacts.

Attachments: pilot-cost-estimate-emu.xlsx (cost model + three commitment tiers), emu-inference-reqs-20260923.pdf (notes from call).

Thanks — we think a 6-week pilot will let us validate the SLOs and show unit economics improvements quickly. Happy to hop on a working session to walk through the traffic sample.

Best,
Kimberly Park
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
[kim@redwood.com]

From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>

Subject: RE: Post-call: inference readiness map + procurement asks

Thanks Kim — echoing the summary and adding the technical breakdown for sizing and the performance knobs we'll use during the pilot. I focused on the latency math and topology tradeoffs so Emu's infra team has something concrete to evaluate.

Assumptions (from call + baseline):
- Avg request tokens (in+out) = 400 tokens per request (180 in, 220 out).
- Target p95 latency = 120ms for full-response generation (server-side generation only; client network latency excluded).
- Peak concurrency window = 220 qps (short spikes ~5–8 minutes); target steady-state concurrency ~35 qps.
- Effective generation throughput per GPU depends on quantization and model size; we used observed perf from our benchmarks.

Suggested pilot topology:
1) Dedicated pool (primary):
   - 6 x A10G nodes (each with 24GB) configured for Redwood-13B-4bit. Estimated sustained QPS per node (with continuous batching + KV cache hit ~30%): ~25–30 qps.
   - Autoscaling headroom: allow +2 nodes for 2x short bursts (fast scale-up; typical spin-up ~60s).
2) Hot-standby H100 instance:
   - 1 x H100 to absorb sudden hot failures and to run heavy-batch offline regen jobs.
3) Hosted API fallback:
   - Use Hosted model variant (same family, slightly higher latency) for overflow beyond Dedicated capacity.

Latency budget break-down (p95 target 120ms):
- Inference generation: 75–90ms (with batching window ~30ms, per-token generation optimized).
- Network + routing + load-balancer: 10–20ms internal (within region).
- Prefetch/KV cache + preprocess: 10–20ms.
- Buffer for jitter: ~5ms.

Batching and cache knobs:
- Continuous batching window: 20–40ms (tunable from pilot telemetry).
- KV-prefix cache: expect 20–35% effective token reduction on repeated triage prompts; this pushes the per-request cost and latency down noticeably.
- Quantization: 4-bit with quantization-aware kernels; metric to watch: qualitative regression on clinical hallucination (we'll run evals).

Estimated pilot capacity and cost (rough):
- Dedicated baseline (6 A10G): steady-state support ~150–180 qps (with caching), burst headroom with +2 nodes and Hosted overflow to cover 220 qps spikes.
- Expected per-request cost (tokens + infra amortized) in pilot: ~$0.0017–0.0024 depending on cache hit rates. We'll refine with trace.

Operational runbook items to confirm during pilot:
- Token retention policy (how long logs are kept; mandatory if PHI present).
- Model rollouts: ability to pin model and rollout canary to 5% before full production.
- Alert SLOs: p95 latency, error rate, and token-per-second cost delta.

Questions for Emu engineering to unblock sizing accuracy:
- Do you have an existing cache key behavior we should align on (i.e., are prompts templated or highly freeform)?
- Are there any spike-protection limits on your side (ingress throttles) we should be aware of?

I'll follow up with a short capacity sketch spreadsheet later tonight (node counts, expected qps per node). If we proceed to Private deployment later, we'll swap dedicated pool for VPC Private control plane and add KMS integration.

-Jonas
Senior Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference
